name: Archetype: industrial mass conscript armies (1850-1918)

weightNotes.aggression: The pre-1914 'cult of the offensive' (Plan XVII, the Schlieffen plan) and repeated mass offensives on the Western Front 1915-17 despite losses (House ch. 1-2; Lupfer). Above middle.
weightNotes.maneuver: Railway mobilisation allowed operational manoeuvre (1866, 1870, Tannenberg 1914), but tactically the war became positional attrition once fronts closed in late 1914 (House ch. 2). Low.
weightNotes.flanking: Wide envelopments were the operational ideal (Sedan 1870, the 1914 Schlieffen wheel, Tannenberg) until continuous fronts removed open flanks. Moderate.
weightNotes.siegePreference: Fortress sieges recurred (Metz and Paris 1870, Plevna 1877, Port Arthur 1904, Liege and Verdun); Verdun 1916 was designed to bleed the enemy at a fortress he had to hold. Low-moderate.
weightNotes.reserveUse: Mass reserve formations mobilised by rail, and from 1917 deliberate counterattack divisions held behind the front in the elastic defence (Lupfer). Moderate.
weightNotes.scouting: Cavalry screens failed against magazine rifles; early aerial reconnaissance helped (Tannenberg, the Marne) but tactical intelligence of enemy depth stayed poor. Low-moderate.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Attacks were pressed through very heavy losses (Somme, 1 July 1916; Verdun), yet armies could also withdraw in order (the 1914 retreat to the Marne, the 1917 Hindenburg Line withdrawal). Moderate-high. Judgment.
weightNotes.combinedArms: 1914 armies coordinated infantry and artillery poorly; by 1917-18 creeping barrages, infiltration tactics, tanks and ground-attack aircraft produced real all-arms battle (House ch. 2; Lupfer). Average across the period.
weightNotes.initiative: Centralised timetables and rigid fire plans; the German army's 1917-18 shift to decentralised stormtroop and defence-in-depth methods is the notable exception (Lupfer). Low.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Armies were tied to railheads; offensives that outran them stalled (the Marne 1914, the 1918 German spring offensives). Moderate-high.

summary: Universal conscription and reserve systems produced armies of millions, mobilised and moved by railway and supplied by industrial economies. Before 1914 doctrine stressed the offensive and moral force; magazine rifles, machine guns and quick-firing artillery made frontal assault ruinously costly, and by late 1914 continuous trench lines from the Channel to Switzerland removed the flanks. The war became one of artillery and attrition, broken only by the slow development of infiltration tactics, elastic defence in depth, creeping barrages, tanks and air support in 1916-18.
whyItWorked: Mass and industry let a state absorb enormous losses and keep fighting for years; railways concentrated reserves faster than any attacker could exploit a breach, which made the defence dominant. Prussia's general staff system turned this into quick decisive wars in 1866 and 1870, and Germany's 1917 elastic defence in depth beat back the Nivelle and Passchendaele offensives (Lupfer).
whereItFailed: Frontal offensives against entrenched machine guns and artillery: the Battles of the Frontiers 1914, Gallipoli 1915, Verdun and the Somme 1916 (about 57,000 British casualties on the first day), the Nivelle offensive and the French mutinies of 1917, Passchendaele 1917. The German 1918 spring offensives broke through tactically but had no mobile exploitation force and outran their railheads.

sources.title: Lupfer, The Dynamics of Doctrine: The Changes in German Tactical Doctrine During the First World War (Leavenworth Paper 4, DTIC ADA563816)
House, Towards Combined Arms Warfare (CSI Research Survey 2, 1984), ch. 1-2
